questions.title: Inferring grazing effects in a rocky pool
questions.stem:
At each of ten comparable pools, researchers randomly assigned two equal rock plots to either a grazer-exclusion cage or an open-sided cage that admitted grazers. Both treatments used the same mesh above the rock. The table gives mean algal dry mass. Values are g m⁻².

| Time | Exclusion | Open-sided |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Start | 18 | 19 |
| Week 2 | 27 | 22 |
| Week 4 | 42 | 24 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the difference between treatments in change from start to week 4, and give its units.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why the open-sided treatment is more informative than simply comparing a caged plot with a bare rock.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why the pool is a sensible unit for pairing plots and identify the independent replicate count.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: State a conclusion supported by the means and one measurement needed to assess consistency among pools.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Suggest a second mechanism besides grazing that could differ between cage types and a way to test it.

steps.text: Exclusion change=42−18=24 g m⁻².
Open-sided change=24−19=5 g m⁻².
Difference in changes=19 g m⁻².
The open-sided cage controls partly for shading or physical disturbance from the cage.
Grazers still enter, so the comparison more closely isolates the effect of excluding grazers.
Plots within one pool share local conditions such as wave exposure or nutrient supply.
Comparing within pools controls some between-pool variation.
There are ten independent pool pairs, not twenty independent pairs.
Exclusion is associated with greater biomass accumulation over four weeks.
Report differences for each pair or their variability/confidence interval to assess consistency.
Closed sides might change water flow or sedimentation.
Measure local flow or sediment deposition with matched instruments or add a design isolating this effect.

questions.title: Two plant glucose polymers
questions.stem: A plant stores glucose in polymer S and uses polymer W to reinforce cell walls. Hydrolysis of purified samples yields glucose in both cases.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify S and W and distinguish their glucose building blocks.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Connect the arrangement of cellulose chains to wall strength.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why storing glucose as starch helps maintain cellular water balance.

steps.text: S is starch.
W is cellulose.
Starch uses α-glucose and cellulose β-glucose.
Alternating glucose orientation produces long straight chains.
Hydrogen bonds form between adjacent chains.
Bundles or microfibrils resist tensile stress.
A large insoluble polymer contributes fewer osmotically active dissolved particles than many free glucose molecules.
This limits osmotic water entry compared with storing the same glucose units as free solute.

questions.title: Interpreting vaccination outcomes
questions.stem: In a randomized trial with complete follow-up, 24 of 800 vaccinated participants and 64 of 800 comparison participants developed laboratory-confirmed disease. Both groups received identical surveillance.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate risk in each group and the relative risk reduction.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Distinguish that reduction from the absolute change in risk. State why random assignment matters.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain how vaccination can reduce disease despite some vaccinated participants still developing it.

steps.text: Vaccinated risk=24/800=3.0% and comparison risk=64/800=8.0%.
Relative risk=0.03/0.08=0.375.
Relative risk reduction=(1−0.375)×100=62.5%.
Absolute reduction=8.0%−3.0%=5.0 percentage points.
Random assignment helps balance prior exposure, age and other confounders between groups.
Antigen exposure can generate specific immune memory and a faster response on infection.
Individuals vary in response and protection can be incomplete, so reduced risk allows breakthrough cases.

questions.title: Reading a sequence of cell images
questions.stem: The time series shows one animal cell in culture. Times are measured from a common starting point. The images do not show individual chromosomes clearly.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe two changes visible between the first and last images.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify the division process directly supported by the shape change and distinguish it from division of a nucleus.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A student claims the images prove the daughter cells have identical DNA sequences. Evaluate the claim and propose evidence.

steps.text: The cell outline becomes constricted near its middle.
Two approximately rounded cell bodies become distinguishable where there was one.
Cytokinesis partitions the cytoplasm, here through cleavage.
Mitosis separates duplicated chromosomes into daughter nuclei.
Chromosomes or DNA sequences cannot be compared at this image resolution.
Normal mitosis predicts similar nuclear genomes but mutation or segregation errors cannot be excluded from shapes.
Compare DNA sequences of the two cells to test sequence identity, or use chromosome analysis specifically to test chromosome complement.

questions.title: Supplying an exercising muscle
questions.stem: A runner begins sustained exercise. Consider the path from air to a working muscle cell and how that cell uses the delivered oxygen.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Outline the main mechanical changes during inspiration in a human at rest.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how the alveolar exchange surface allows rapid transfer of oxygen into blood.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain how increased oxygen delivery supports sustained movement, linking transport to energy transfer.

parts.label: quality
parts.prompt: Quality of the complete extended response

steps.text: The diaphragm contracts and flattens.
External intercostal contraction raises the ribs, increasing thoracic volume.
Pressure in the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure, causing inward airflow.
Many alveoli provide a large surface area.
Thin alveolar walls and thin capillary walls create a short diffusion distance.
A moist surface permits oxygen to dissolve.
Ventilation replenishes alveolar oxygen.
Blood flow removes oxygenated blood and maintains a partial-pressure gradient for diffusion.
Oxygen binds reversibly to haemoglobin in red cells.
The left heart pumps oxygenated blood into systemic arteries.
Blood reaches capillaries near muscle fibres.
Respiring fibres maintain a lower oxygen concentration or partial pressure than incoming blood.
Oxygen dissociates and diffuses into the tissues.
Aerobic respiration transfers chemical energy from organic substrates into ATP with a high yield compared with anaerobic release.
ATP supplies energy for contraction; continuing delivery and substrate supply support repeated cycles.

questions.title: Variation, selection and conservation
questions.stem: An isolated lizard population varies in a heritable trait affecting survival on hot rock. A conservation scheme will establish a second population.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Outline sources of genetic variation in sexually reproducing organisms.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how directional selection could change the trait distribution over many generations.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Discuss choices that would help the second population retain diversity and allow the conservation team to assess its success.

parts.label: quality
parts.prompt: Quality of the complete extended response

steps.text: Mutation creates new alleles.
Meiosis produces new allele combinations by independent assortment or crossing over.
Random union of gametes creates additional combinations.
Individuals initially differ in the trait.
Some variants tolerate the hot surface better.
They survive or reproduce more successfully under those conditions.
Their heritable variants are transmitted disproportionately to offspring.
The advantageous variants increase in frequency across generations if the selective conditions persist.
Choose founders across the source population rather than a single family.
Include enough unrelated breeders to represent multiple alleles.
A small founder sample can lose rare alleles by chance.
Small subsequent populations can lose further variation by drift or inbreeding.
Provide suitable habitat and resources for successful reproduction.
Monitor survival and recruitment over several generations rather than counting released adults alone.
Compare genetic diversity or allele frequencies over time and adapt management if diversity declines.
